1.pericope_label: The eighteen-month siege, the famine, the breach, and the trial and blinding of Zedekiah at Riblah

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the parallel, noting that the narrative agrees exactly with Jeremiah’s throughout.

Henry reads the siege theologically: Jerusalem once compassed with God’s favour as with a shield and now left defenceless, a city punished for its fulness of bread, and a king whose flight proves that those who think to escape God’s judgments deceive themselves as much as those who brave them.

Clarke dates the entry and the flight, and reconstructs the campaign from Jeremiah; Wesley explains the siege works, makes the starving people the commons rather than the great men, and sets the two seemingly contrary prophecies about Babylon side by side.

Ellicott works the dates, the siege vocabulary, the defective Hebrew of the fourth verse, the topography of the gate between the two walls and the plains of Jericho, and the singular verbs of the sentence; Delitzsch reckons the siege at eighteen months, finds a copyist’s oversight in the missing month, and traces the trial to the broken oath.

debates.question: Which month does the third verse name, and why is it missing?

sides.position: a copyist's oversight: the words naming the fourth month fell out before the day
supplied from Jeremiah, though a Syriac text reads the fifth month and may be original

debates.question: Who are the people of the land for whom there was no bread?

sides.position: the civil population, especially families crowded in from the country, against Thenius
the commons, as distinct from the great men
the militia, which Ellicott answers are the men of war of the next verse

debates.question: Who blinded Zedekiah and carried him off?

sides.position: Jeremiah's verbs are singular, so the acts fall to Nebuchadnezzar, though not necessarily by his own hand
the Chaldaeans who took him, acting on the sentence passed at Riblah

outliers: Ellicott alone works the siege vocabulary, noting that the word rendered forts occurs only in Ezekiel, means some siege work nobody can specify, and comes out as wall in the Greek and palisade in the Syriac.

Wesley alone sets beside the sentence the two predictions that seemed to contradict, that the king should go to Babylon yet never see it, which the false prophet of the same name could not reconcile and so called both false.
Henry alone reads the encircling theologically, Jerusalem once compassed with God's favour as with a shield and now left without defence.
themes: a siege dated to the day and kept as a fast
eighteen months and what the fortifications must have been
a famine recorded as proof of prophecy
a gate between two walls by the king’s garden
a trial for a broken oath

8.pericope_label: Nebuzaradan burns the temple and city, breaks the walls, strips the brass, and the chief officers are slain at Riblah

schools.summary: Gill flags the discrepancy over the day of the burning and refuses Benjamin of Tudela’s story about the pillars at Rome.

Henry gives the burning its longest reflection, a holy and beautiful house not fire-proof against judgment, a temple trusted as protection and found a refuge of lies, signs left standing after the thing signified was sinned away, and a ministration ended with the vessels that served it.

Clarke resolves the date by chronology and reckons the five men against Jeremiah’s seven; Wesley takes the month’s delay for a space to repent, dismisses the apocryphal story of the hidden ark, and observes that the poor had liberty at home while the rich went prisoners abroad.

Ellicott corrects the text and the English throughout, from the numeral of the day to the copper that is called brass and the capital of three cubits that should be five, and identifies the condemned officers; Delitzsch heads and divides the section and explains why the colossal vessels were broken up.

debates.question: Was the temple burnt on the seventh day of the month or the tenth?

sides.position: the seventh is an error for the tenth, one numeral letter mistaken for another
both: entry on the seventh, two days provisioning, firing on the tenth
the discrepancy between this text and Jeremiah is flagged and left

debates.question: How many men of the king’s presence were taken?

sides.position: five in the Greek, Syriac and Vulgate, fifty in the Targum, seven in Jeremiah; a numeral partly obliterated
five, Jeremiah reaching seven by counting in the war-officer and the scribe of the host

debates.question: Why were the threescore men of the land taken with the officers?

sides.position: they were what remained of the citadel garrison
they had distinguished themselves in the defence, or were ringleaders of the revolt

debates.question: Why did the king of Babylon put them all to death?

sides.position: he had found that they counselled Zedekiah to revolt
he was too irritated by the obstinacy of their defence to admire their bravery
divine justice saw in them the ringleaders of the idolatry

outliers: Gill alone reports Benjamin of Tudela’s claim that the two pillars stand in a church at Rome with Solomon’s name engraved and sweat every ninth of Ab, and refuses it on the ground that this verse says they were broken in pieces.

Henry alone reads the removal of the brass as a sign cancelled, Jachin and Boaz having stood for the strength and stability of the house, so that when the thing signified was sinned away the signs had no business standing.
Ellicott alone compares the hyperbole of brass without weight with the Assyrian boast of spoils without number.
Delitzsch alone explains the breaking up on practical grounds, that the colossal pieces could hardly be moved whole.
themes: a month of patience between the capture and the burning
a temple that was not fire-proof against judgment
the common houses spared for the poor
brass that should probably be read as copper
a capital of three cubits that should be five
the sagan who served for a disabled high priest

22.pericope_label: Gedaliah set over the remnant and murdered, the flight into Egypt, and Jehoiachin lifted up at Babylon

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the chronology and the company, dating the murder near two months after the fall and adding Baruch and the king’s daughters to those who went down into Egypt.

Henry defends Gedaliah, blames the murder on spite against the Chaldeans, thinks the flight into Egypt the real end of the nation, and reads Jehoiachin’s release three ways: as a dawn, as a generous act, and as a providence timed at the midnight of the captivity.

Clarke deflates the governorship to an overseer’s charge, supplies the sequel of the murder from Jeremiah, and has the released king keep a court in Babylon until he fell with his protector; Wesley finds the motive in envy and guesses the refugees were absorbed into Egypt.

Ellicott vindicates Gedaliah as a disciple of Jeremiah, dates and motivates the murder, and works the philology and chronology of Evil-merodach’s accession and the precedence given the captive king; Delitzsch narrates the assassination, blames similar letters for the disputed day, and refuses the inference that Jehoiachin died first.

sides.position: no regal dignity, but an overseer set to regulate the husbandmen left behind
a governorship, and he a disciple of Jeremiah who might have blessed the people more than their kings did

debates.question: Where was the Mizpah he lived in?

sides.position: the Benjamite Mizpah, high and strong, with an ancient sanctuary that might serve for the ruined temple
reported east of Jordan and nearest Babylon, though several places bore the name
the assassin was of the seed royal and thought his claim better, with the Ammonite king behind him
envy at seeing so mean a person advanced into their place
spite against the Chaldeans, because the governor was their appointment

debates.question: Did Jehoiachin die before his benefactor?

sides.position: yes, falling with his protector when that king was killed in a conspiracy two years later
the text does not warrant the inference, since the favour might have been continued by a successor

outliers: Ellicott alone reads the precedence over the other captive kings as a higher chair of state in the royal hall, recalling Cyrus keeping Croesus at court.
Wesley alone guesses what became of the refugees, mixed by degrees with the Egyptians and heard of no more as Israelites.
Henry alone reports the Jewish tradition that Evil-merodach had himself been imprisoned by his father and there made friends with Jehoiachin, and dates the kindness to the midnight of the captivity.
Ellicott alone reads the closing verses as a faint gleam the writer dwells on with pleasure, foreshadowing the pity later shown the captive people.
themes: a governor defended against the charge of treachery
a sanctuary standing in for a burnt temple
a friendly meal and a murder
a remnant that fled the land it still held
a head lifted up out of prison
thirty-six of the seventy years gone
